title: Elodie and the Bell
premise: Urban explorer Casper Whitlock returns to their dying hometown to sell the family house and finds the imaginary friend of their childhood, Elodie, waiting on the porch — unchanged after twenty years. Elodie drags them into a buried network of tunnels beneath the town where a bell tolls a song that keeps something ancient asleep, and where the town's founders long ago bargained lives for safety: every harvest moon, someone must sing along and be taken. Casper, who has never believed in anything, must learn the song's forbidden last verse from Elodie without singing it aloud, while falling for the town's reluctant bell-keeper, Mara Voss, whose duty is to choose each year's sacrifice. In the climax under the harvest moon, Casper refuses both options — sing or flee — and instead rings the bell themselves with Elodie's name woven into the verse, breaking the bargain at the cost of Elodie's existence; the thing below wakes briefly, is named, and dissolves. The town survives, changed and grieving, and Casper stays, choosing found family over escape.
about_author: Odile Okafor is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent a decade cataloguing sealed basements and unlisted utility tunnels before turning to horror. They write about small towns that keep their bargains quietly.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Returning to Hollow Creek to empty the family house, Casper finds the porch light burning and Elodie — their childhood imaginary friend, ageless and unchanged — sitting on the steps. The emotional beat is uncanny dread braided with a shameful flicker of joy.

chapters.title: What the Survey Missed
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper rationalizes, photographs Elodie, and maps the cellar door that opens onto stairs no blueprint records. Elodie only says, 'You came back before the moon.' The beat is denial hardening into compulsion.

chapters.title: Bell-Keeper's Hours
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Introduces Mara Voss, who tends the old meetinghouse bell and keeps a ledger of names going back two centuries. She notices Casper asking questions and warns them off with practiced coldness. The beat is duty masking fear.

chapters.title: Down Where the Air Hums
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. First descent: tunnels of dressed stone beneath the town, walls scored with tally marks, air humming faintly with melody. Casper hears a second voice humming along and runs. The beat is wonder curdling into violation.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara finds her own grandmother's name circled in the ledger and recalls the night she was chosen as keeper as a girl. She decides to watch Casper. The beat is inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Elodie Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Elodie reveals she was real once — a child taken by the bargain generations ago, sustained below until she slipped out through a lonely kid's imagination. She needs Casper to learn the last verse. The beat is betrayal reframed as plea.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on the town. Preparations for the festival: wreaths, shutters, the meetinghouse bell wrapped in cloth so it cannot ring early. The beat is communal complicity, everyone smiling too widely.

chapters.title: First Verse
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Mara catches Casper in the tunnels and, instead of reporting them, teaches the first two verses — the safe ones — explaining the rule: learn, never sing. Attraction sparks between them. The beat is wary alliance becoming intimacy.

chapters.title: The One Who Sang Along
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Flashback chapter: last year's harvest, when Mara's brother Theo sang along deliberately to spare a child, and what walked him down the stairs smiling. The beat is grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: Tally Marks
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Casper counts the tunnel tallies and realizes they mark years since the thing below last woke fully — and that one wall's marks stop mid-century, the year Elodie was taken. The beat is history becoming personal.

chapters.title: The Founder's Bargain
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. In the archive, Mara and Casper find the founders' contract: safety in exchange for a singer each harvest moon, renewed by whoever rings the bell. The current signature line is blank — waiting. The beat is horror of paperwork.

chapters.title: Second Verse, Wrong Key
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Practicing alone, Casper hums a bar too low and the tunnels answer; doors in town open onto darkness all night. Mara covers for them. The beat is consequence and deepening trust.

chapters.title: Elodie's Hunger
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Elodie grows strange, translucent at the edges, pressing Casper to hurry — and Casper suspects Elodie's freedom requires a replacement singer. The beat is love for an imaginary friend shadowed by suspicion.

chapters.title: Cloth Off the Bell
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Someone unwraps the bell overnight; it tolls once, unstruck, and every dog in Hollow Creek goes silent. The town looks at Mara. The beat is a community turning on its keeper.

chapters.title: The Candidate
chapters.summary: Third person alternating. The town council, desperate, selects a singer: a newcomer with no ties — meaning Casper. Mara is ordered to deliver them. The beat is duty and love colliding head-on.

chapters.title: Last Verse, Half-Learned
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Elodie teaches the final verse in fragments, but refuses to finish it — the last lines, she admits, are the thing's own name, and singing them frees or destroys. The beat is knowledge as a loaded gun.

chapters.title: Night Before the Moon
chapters.summary: Mara and Casper's shared POV. On the meetinghouse roof, Mara offers Casper her truck and a head start; Casper offers to stay and face it together. They choose each other, badly and completely. The beat is love against duty, consummated in defiance.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The town gathers at the mouth of the stairs; Elodie leads Casper down toward the bell chamber below, where the humming has become a choir. The beat is procession into the dark, terrible and calm.

chapters.title: The Bell Below
chapters.summary: Climax, Casper's POV. Offered the choice — sing along and live as the next keeper, or run — Casper seizes the rope and rings the bell while speaking the last verse, weaving Elodie's true name into it. The thing below rises, is fully named, and comes apart like smoke. Elodie brightens, thanks them, and unravels into the ringing. The beat is sacrifice, naming, and release.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Silence
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Dawn: the tunnels are ordinary stone, the ledger's pages blank, the town furious and freed in equal measure. Mara takes the blame and the credit. The beat is exhausted reckoning.

chapters.title: What Casper Kept
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Packing the house, Casper finds a chalk drawing from childhood — Elodie's — now signed with a full name and a date, proof she existed. They decide not to sell. The beat is mourning made bearable by evidence of love.

chapters.title: The New Song
chapters.summary: Shared epilogue POV. A year later, Casper and Mara teach the town a new song at the harvest festival — one written, not inherited — and ring the bell because they choose to, not because they must. The beat is found family, chosen ritual, quiet hope.
